text: open-label study.26 However, the use of sirolimus with mycophenolate mofetil was associated with a higher than expected incidence of acute rejection in car- diac transplant patients switched from calcineurin inhibi- tors to this combination.27 It has been suggested that the high doses of corticosteroids used increase the risk of cardiac adverse events in the long- er term, and protocols that wean patients from corticoster- oids after 6 months postoperatively have been used,28,29 without apparent increases in infection or rejection. Corti- costeroid avoidance or early withdrawal regimens are fea- sible in many, if not most, paediatric heart transplant recip- ients.9 In the early post-transplant period, the most significant causes of morbidity are infection and rejection epi- sodes.8,9 Other complications post-transplant include right ventricular failure and cardiac arrhythmias.30 Co-trimoxa- zole is used to protect against Pneumocystis jirovecii infec- tion, and ganciclovir as prophylaxis against CMV.3 Rejec- tion is usually treated with corticosteroids, but other drugs have been used for corticosteroid-resistant cases,8 includ- ing antilymphocyte immunoglobulins and muromonab- CD3.4,29 In repetitive rejection, tacrolimus may be substi- tuted for ciclosporin, and mycophenolate mofetil for aza- thioprine.4,5 Adjunctive methotrexate, total lymphoid irra- diation and photopheresis have all been tried.8 In the late post-transplant period, malignancy and coro- nary artery disease are the most significant problems.3,7,8 About 5% of paediatric heart transplant recipients have been reported to develop post-transplant lymphoprolifera- tive disease (PTLD).2,31 The strongest risk factor for PTLD is the development of primary Epstein-Barr virus infection after transplantation although children who are seroposi- tive for the virus are not necessarily protected from this complication.2,9 Despite treatment with chemotherapy or a reduction in immunosuppression, PTLD is associated with significant morbidity and mortality; acute rejection may occur in those whose immunosuppression is reduced.2 Rituximab and cellular immunotherapy are novel thera- peutic approaches for PTLD.9 Cardiac allograft vasculop- athy (also termed coronary artery vasculopathy, or chronic rejection) is a major cause of death and prevention of its progression is a major therapeutic goal.2,3,9,32,33 It is thought to be mainly an immunological response, but can be accelerated by the classical risk factors of dyslipidae- mia, obesity, glucose intolerance, and smoking, as well as by postoperative CMV infection, and immunosuppression itself.3,6,8,34 Long-term use of calcineurin inhibitors is as-
